newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Council backs plan for U.N.-run Croatian enclave.
newsitem.headline: Council backs plan for U.N.-run Croatian enclave.

text.p: The Security Council on Friday issued a last call to Serbs in the Eastern Slavonia enclave to accept crucial pledges from Zagreb for their future before the region reverts to Croatia later this year.

The once-volatile region, dominated by Serbs and bordering the Yugoslav republic of Serbia, is the only remaining Croatian area not under Zagreb's control. A U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) has been administering the area for about a year to prevent any resumption of fighting.

In a statement read at a formal meeting, the council said that Zagreb's guarantees, negotiated at length with the United Nations, constituted a "solid basis" for holding elections, tentatively scheduled for March 16.
"The council underlines the need for full cooperation by the local Serbs," said the statement, which at the same time told Croatia to "implement fully" its commitments.

Croatia has promised citizenship to Serbs living in the area since January 1996, Serb representation at various levels of local, and national government bodies, access to social services and educational and cultural autonomy.
In addition, the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia are exempt from military service for two years and can apply for conscientious objector service after that.
So far Serb leaders in the enclave, despite urging from Jacques Klein, the American diplomat in charge of the region for the United Nations, protested Croatia's promises.

They want permanent demilitarization of the enclave, exemption from military service for at least 15 years, guarantees to remain in their present homes until their original houses are rebuilt and the creation of a separate political "county" for the region.

The 5,000 U.N. troops are to begin leaving Croatia 30 days after the elections and be gone by July 1. After that civilian monitors and some military observers are expected to remain for at least another six months.
Both Klein and Secretary-General Kofi Annan have urged local Serbs to put aside "unrealistic demands."

There are anywhere between 110,000 and 140,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, many of whom fled from other Serb-dominated areas of Croatia during Zagreb's military offensive in the summer of 1995. Croatia says about 56,000 have applied for documents and about 46,000 have been issued.
Klein told reporters it was necessary that the council send a "clear signal" to the Serbs. "I think the Serbs need to hear that message because there are always some who delay."
"They don't like the idea of living in Croatia," he added. "I understand that, but at the same time we have to move forward. I think it is a very fair, good, package."
The elections, to coincide with polls throughout Croatia, would include voting booths throughout the republic to accommodate all the Croatian refugees, he said.

The council also encouraged Croatia to maintain the current demilitarized status of the region but it failed to approve Klein's proposal that Serbia should do likewise in some areas on its side of the border, diplomats said.

Klein, at times by the sheer force of his personality, is credited with making inroads in the Serb population, such as organising as recruiting police to serve with Croatia police, starting programmes to reunite families and driving corrupt Serb militias from the enclave and its oil fields.
